recipe.history:
Chile relleno — literally "stuffed chile" in Spanish — is one of the crown jewels of Mexican cuisine, tracing its roots back to the city of Puebla, Mexico, at least as far as the 16th century. The dish is fundamentally an expression of indigenous Mesoamerican cooking traditions fused with Spanish colonial influence: the poblano pepper, named for the very same city, was a cornerstone crop of the region long before European contact, while the technique of stuffing it with cheese — typically queso Oaxaca or queso fresco — and bathing it in a light egg batter before frying reflects the Spanish introduction of dairy and refined frying methods. Classic chile relleno is then draped in a gently spiced tomato-based ranchero sauce, which ties the whole dish together with a warm, earthy sweetness. It is a dish that rewards patience and technique in equal measure, and in Puebla it is considered as much a point of cultural pride as mole poblano itself.

The flavors of chile relleno made their way into American cuisine through the centuries-long culinary dialogue between Mexico and the American Southwest — a conversation shaped by geography, migration, and the relentless human appetite for bold flavor. As Tex-Mex and Cal-Mex traditions evolved through the 20th century, cooks began deconstructing and reimagining classic Mexican dishes in the context of American comfort food. The burger, being the most democratic of American canvases, was an inevitable destination. The combination of a charred, savory poblano pepper with molten, stretchy cheese and a rich battered crust mapped naturally onto the burger's own architecture of heat, fat, and umami. By the time Bob Belcher was writing specials on his chalkboard, the chile relleno burger had already found a home in food trucks and diners across California, Texas, and New Mexico — a cross-cultural mashup that honors both traditions without diminishing either.

I first encountered something like this burger at a roadside stand outside of Albuquerque on a trip I took with my father when I was twelve years old. It was the kind of place with a hand-painted sign, a single propane grill, and a line of people who clearly knew something I didn't. My father, who never ordered anything more adventurous than a plain cheeseburger back home, pointed at the board and said, "that one" without hesitation. What arrived was messy, magnificent, and completely unlike anything I had tasted before — the poblano half-melted into the patty, cheese oozing from its split seam, the whole thing unified by a smear of something smoky and red that I later learned was a simple ancho sauce. I didn't have the vocabulary for it then. I just knew I wanted it again. I have been chasing that particular afternoon ever since, and every time I make this burger I get a little closer to catching it.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a beef burger patty, and it is medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, or roughly 54 to 57 degrees Celsius. This is not a matter of opinion or preference — it is a matter of physics, chemistry, and respect for the animal. At medium rare, the fat within the grind has begun to render and lubricate the meat fibers without fully escaping, which means every bite is juicy, beefy, and cohesive. The proteins have set just enough to hold the patty together while retaining a yielding, almost silken interior texture. Anything cooked beyond this point is, by definition, drier, tougher, and less flavorful — the fat has fled, the juices have been wrung out, and what remains is a disc of compacted protein that has forgotten what it used to be. A medium rare patty respects the entire chain of effort — the farmer, the butcher, the grind, the seasoning — by refusing to undo it at the last moment. Cook to 130°F. Use a thermometer. Do not apologize.
ingredients: 200g queso Oaxaca, shredded (or low-moisture mozzarella as substitute)
Vegetable oil for frying (enough for 2 inches depth in pan)
3 dried ancho chiles, stemmed and seeded
60ml mayonnaise (homemade preferred: 1 egg yolk, 1 tsp Dijon, 1 tsp white wine vinegar, 120ml neutral oil, salt)
1 tsp adobo sauce from the can
1 small white onion, thinly sliced into rings
1 cup whole milk (for soaking onion rings)
4 leaves iceberg or green leaf lettuce
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg. Knead with dough hook on medium 8–10 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise at room temperature until doubled, about 90 minutes.

2. Punch down dough, divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 130g each), and shape into tight rounds. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover loosely, and proof a second time for 45–60 minutes until noticeably puffed.

3. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns with egg wash (1 yolk + 1 tbsp milk) and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake 15–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool completely on a wire rack before slicing.

4. Make the ranchero sauce: Place tomato halves cut-side up, jalapeño, onion, and unpeeled garlic on a foil-lined baking sheet. Broil on high 10–12 minutes until charred in spots. Meanwhile, toast ancho chiles in a dry skillet over medium heat 30 seconds per side until fragrant. Transfer to a bowl, cover with boiling water, and soak 15 minutes.

5. Peel the roasted garlic. Drain the soaked anchos. Blend the roasted vegetables, drained chiles, chicken stock, cumin, oregano, salt, and pepper until smooth. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a saucepan over medium-high, pour in the blended sauce (it will spit), and cook stirring frequently for 10–12 minutes until darkened and thickened to a loose gravy consistency. Adjust seasoning and keep warm.

6. Make the chipotle crema: If making mayonnaise from scratch, whisk egg yolk, Dijon, and vinegar in a bowl, then slowly drizzle in neutral oil while whisking constantly until emulsified; season with salt. Blend sour cream, mayo, chipotles, adobo sauce, lime juice, and garlic powder until completely smooth. Taste and adjust heat and salt. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Roast the poblanos: Place poblanos directly over a gas flame or under a broiler, turning with tongs, until completely blackened and blistered on all sides, about 8–10 minutes. Transfer to a bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and steam 15 minutes. Peel off the charred skin under running water — do not rinse away all the char flavor, just the loose skin. Pat dry.

8. Make a slit lengthwise down one side of each peeled poblano, keeping the stem intact. Carefully remove seeds and veins with a spoon. Mix shredded Oaxaca, crumbled queso fresco, cumin, smoked paprika, and garlic powder together. Stuff each poblano generously with the cheese mixture and press the edges closed. Set aside.

9. Make the egg batter: In a clean bowl, beat egg whites with cream of tartar and salt until stiff peaks form. In a separate bowl, lightly beat the yolks. Gently fold yolks into whites, then fold in flour until just combined — the batter should be light and airy, not deflated.

10. Heat 2 inches of vegetable oil in a deep skillet or Dutch oven to 350°F (175°C). Working one at a time, dip each stuffed poblano into the egg batter, coating completely. Gently lower into the oil and fry 2–3 minutes per side until golden and puffed. Drain on a wire rack over a sheet pan and keep warm in a 200°F oven.

11. Make the crispy onion rings: Soak sliced onion rings in milk for 15 minutes. Mix flour, cayenne, garlic powder, and salt in a shallow bowl. Heat oil to 365°F (185°C). Drain onion rings from milk, dredge in seasoned flour, shake off excess, and fry in batches 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp. Drain on a wire rack, season immediately with flaky salt.

12. Form and cook the patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 150g each). Gently form into patties about 4.5 inches wide and 3/4-inch thick — handle as little as possible. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and black pepper immediately before cooking.

13. Heat a cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties without pressing or moving them for 3 minutes. Flip once and cook another 2–3 minutes. Begin checking internal temperature at the 2-minute mark on the second side. Pull patties at exactly 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack 2–3 minutes — they will carry over to a perfect rosy interior.
14. While patties rest, slice buns in half and toast cut-side down in the residual fat in the skillet for 60–90 seconds until golden and slightly crispy.

15. Assemble the burgers: Spread chipotle crema generously on both cut sides of the toasted bun. On the bottom bun, lay a leaf of lettuce, followed by tomato slices. Place the rested medium-rare patty on top, season with a pinch of flaky sea salt.

16. Set a battered, fried chile relleno directly on top of the patty — the residual heat from the patty will keep the cheese molten. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of warm ranchero sauce directly over the chile relleno, letting it pool and drip down the sides.

17. Top with a few slices of avocado and a tangle of crispy onion rings. Press the top bun down gently. Serve immediately with lime wedges on the side and extra ranchero sauce for dipping. Do not let this burger sit — it is at its absolute peak in the first two minutes after assembly.
